business_summary: Indian Energy Exchange operates in the power exchange sector. In FY26 it earned an operating margin of 84.46% and net profit of 473.71 Rs cr. Revenue grew 14.92% a year over three years. It carries almost no debt (debt/equity 0.01x). The evidence supplied does not describe its products or volumes.
why_own: The case rests on a high-margin, low-debt business that has compounded revenue at about 15% a year with ROCE of 47.58% and ROE of 39.4%. No investor documents were supplied, so the drivers are metric-only and the qualitative side of the thesis is untested.

drivers.statement: Revenue keeps compounding at a double-digit rate (3-year CAGR currently 14.92%, 5-year 13.92%). (warn line tightened by code from 10 to 10.44.)
Operating margin stays near its current very high level (84.46%, up 0.48 pp over 3 years).
Returns on capital remain high (ROCE 47.58%, ROE 39.4%) with negligible borrowings.
Reported profit is backed by cash: cash from operations was 0.9x net profit in FY26.

kill_criteria.description: Operating margin falls below 65%, well outside the current range.
ROCE falls below 20%, less than half the current level.

risks.statement: The trailing P/E of 19.02x is 49.69% below the stock's own 5-year median. The evidence does not say why, so whether this reflects a cheaper entry point or a changed view of the business is untested. Price/book is 7.09x.
An operating margin of 84.46% leaves limited room for improvement, so profit growth depends mostly on revenue growth. The 3-year net profit CAGR is 17.41% against revenue growth of 14.92%.
Cash conversion is below 1x (0.9x), so some profit was not matched by operating cash in FY26. The cause is not given in the evidence.

skeptic_counter_case: The thesis is built on backward-looking metrics, and its thresholds are loose. Revenue growth would have to fall from 14.92% to below 6% before D1 breaks, and ROCE from 47.58% to below 25% before D3 breaks. The market has already halved the P/E, to 19.02x against a 37.8x median, and the thesis cannot explain why. The supplied transcripts show that power market coupling and the draft market rules are live issues, and the thesis does not test them. The thesis is wrong if regulatory change cuts exchange volumes or pricing, or if profit growth leans on non-operating items rather than on revenue. What would change this view: Evidence that the final market rules and the coupling procedure leave exchange volumes and pricing largely unchanged, together with a breakdown showing profit growth comes from operations rather than other income.
